title: Global Funds Lose Faith in India as Some Cut Stock Allocations to Zero
excerpt: Money managers at Janus Henderson and Vantage Point have pared India exposure to zero, and foreign portfolio ownership has tumbled to a 17-year low as AI-rich North Asia steals the flows.
body:
• India is now the least-favoured market in Asia in Bank of America surveys, and foreign portfolio ownership of NSE-listed companies has fallen to a 17-year low.
  • Money managers at Janus Henderson and Vantage Point Asset Management have cut India exposure to zero over the past year; foreign funds have pulled a net $25 billion from Indian stocks this year.
  • The exodus reflects the absence of an AI investment theme, lukewarm earnings, rich valuations — the Nifty 50 trades at a 77% premium to MSCI's emerging-market benchmark — and a weak rupee amid high oil prices.
  • Domestic institutions have cushioned the fall with about $60 billion of purchases, and Morgan Stanley sees the Sensex rising 19% to 89,000 by next June in its base case.

A market that lost its shine

When Reed Capital Partners decided to trim equity exposure about a month ago, it exited its Indian portfolio entirely. For chief investment officer Gerald Gan, it was an easy call — the India growth story, in his view, is withering away.

His skepticism mirrors a broader retreat. India now ranks as the least-favoured market in Asia in a Bank of America investor survey, and money managers at Janus Henderson Investors and Vantage Point Asset Management said they have pared India exposure to zero over the past year or so. Foreign portfolio ownership of companies listed on the National Stock Exchange of India has tumbled to a 17-year low.

"There isn't much going on for a good India story. It is more the growth story that is withering away for India."

— Gerald Gan, Chief Investment Officer, Reed Capital Partners

Why the money is leaving

Three forces are driving the exodus. The first is the absence of an artificial-intelligence investment theme in India. India's high growth and Modi's infrastructure build-out were once the big draws; that promise now pales beside the AI-driven returns of South Korea and Taiwan. "Many wealth managers have taken India back to underweight or completely out as they are more concerned about covering the increased weighting of tech plays in Taiwan and South Korea," said Gary Dugan, chief executive of Dubai-based Global CIO Office. About 30% of his firm's clients — family offices and wealth managers — have exited India entirely, Dugan said.

The second is valuation. Indian equities trade at about 17.6 times forward earnings — below their historic average but still far more expensive than emerging-market peers. The Nifty 50 commands a 77% valuation premium to MSCI's emerging-market benchmark, prompting foreign funds to pull a net $25 billion this year. The selling resumed in September: foreign investors pulled ₹7,443 crore from Indian equities in the first week despite stronger-than-expected 7.8% April-June GDP growth, Outlook Business reported, taking 2026 outflows to ₹2.32 lakh crore — already above the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in all of 2025.

The third is macro risk. The outbreak of the US-Iran war sent crude prices surging — Brent recently topped $100 a barrel — and pushed the rupee to a record low, among Asia's worst performers this year, despite India raising $127 billion from its diaspora to bolster its currency defences. "The result has been pressure on the current account balance and a weaker rupee," said Carlos Casanova, senior Asia economist at Union Bancaire Privee. A weaker rupee erodes dollar returns for foreign investors, compounding the selling.

The other side of the trade

Not everyone is giving up. Domestic institutions have provided a floor, with net purchases of about $60 billion this year, according to BSE data. Morgan Stanley says India is in a multi-quarter growth upcycle and, in its base case, sees the Sensex rising 19% to 89,000 by June next year.

"Modi came in. He did some positive things that were done very well and within a reasonable timeframe, such as GST harmonization, the real estate reform, the bankruptcy court, but that hasn't solved the real issue," said Sat Duhra, a portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors. "The issue is jobs, it's trying to build manufacturing, trying to gain the FDI."

The Nifty 50 now languishes near its mid-2024 level and is on track to snap a decade-long streak of annual gains — a run bettered among major global markets only by Japan's Nikkei 225 in the 1980s. India's weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index has shrunk to about 11% from 16% a year ago — itself fueling selling, as benchmark-conscious managers find less reason to own it.

What is next

Near-term flows hinge on crude prices, U.S. bond yields and the dollar. Structurally, the question is whether India can manufacture an AI story of its own or reform enough to justify its premium. Until then, the market that was once Asia's hottest destination will have to prove itself the hard way — through earnings.

nri_angle: India raised $127 billion from its diaspora to defend the rupee, showing how directly overseas Indians are being pulled into the country's currency battle — and NRI portfolios tied to Indian equities are feeling the foreign exodus first-hand.
author: Diaspora Desk
